desc:
Every cell of the m x n matrix grid has a positive cost grid[r][c] that you pay each time you step onto the cell. You start on the top-left cell (paying its cost) and want to stand on the bottom-right cell.

From a cell you may move to any of the four side-adjacent cells (up, down, left or right), not only right and down. Return the minimum total cost of a walk from the top-left to the bottom-right cell, counting the cost of every cell on the walk including both ends.

grid = [[1, 1, 1, 1],
        [9, 9, 9, 1],
        [1, 1, 1, 1],
        [1, 9, 9, 9],
        [1, 1, 1, 1]]
best walk snakes right, down, left, down, right: cost 14
(the best walk that only goes right and down costs 16)
hints: The classic dynamic programme for 'minimum path sum' only allows moves to the right and down. Why does that break down when you may also go up and left?
The grid is a graph: cells are vertices, and stepping onto a cell costs that cell's value. All costs are positive, so shortest-path algorithms apply.
Run Dijkstra from the top-left cell with initial distance grid[0][0]. Relax each neighbour with d + grid[nr][nc]. Return the distance of the bottom-right cell when it is popped.
editorial: With four-direction movement a cheap cell can lie 'behind' you, so the cost of a cell no longer depends only on its top and left neighbours and the simple DP table cannot be filled in one sweep. Treat the grid as a graph with up to 3,600 vertices: the weight of entering a cell is that cell's cost.

Dijkstra's algorithm handles it: keep dist[r][c] initialised to infinity except dist[0][0] = grid[0][0], pop the smallest (d, r, c) from a min-heap, skip stale entries, and relax the four neighbours. The first time the bottom-right cell is popped its distance is optimal because all costs are positive.
Time is O(mn log(mn)) and space O(mn). For a 1 x 1 grid the answer is just the single cell's cost.
